content: The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) approved a new rapid test for detecting HIV antibodies in 2002, as reported in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR). The global TB database for 2023 provides a comprehensive profile of the disease's burden worldwide. WHO has issued consolidated guidelines for treating drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB, emphasizing the importance of rapid communication and updated treatment protocols. A multicountry analysis published in PLoS Medicine in 2020 examined the prevalence and genetic profiles of isoniazid resistance in TB patients, highlighting the need for targeted interventions. Similarly, WHO has developed a catalog of mutations in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex associated with drug resistance, aiding in the identification of extensively drug-resistant TB. Population-based surveillance studies have revealed resistance patterns to key TB drugs, such as pyrazinamide and fluoroquinolones, underscoring the need for advanced diagnostic tools. WHO has also released technical reports on critical concentrations for drug susceptibility testing, particularly for isoniazid and rifamycins, to guide treatment decisions. Genetic sequencing has been identified as a valuable tool for monitoring drug resistance in high-burden countries. The development of target product profiles (TPPs) for TB diagnostics has been a collaborative effort involving public consultations and expert input. These TPPs aim to define the characteristics of next-generation diagnostic tests, including rapid detection of TB and drug resistance at peripheral healthcare centers. Stakeholders have emphasized the importance of affordability, accessibility, and high diagnostic accuracy, particularly in resource-limited settings. Operational characteristics of TB diagnostics, such as ease of use, rapid turnaround times, and minimal maintenance requirements, have been prioritized. For example, the optimal time-to-result for TB tests has been set at less than 30 minutes, with a preference for instrument-free, point-of-care solutions. The cost of diagnostic instruments and tests has been a key consideration, with efforts to balance affordability and innovation. The WHO has also highlighted the importance of connectivity in diagnostic technologies to improve surveillance and accelerate TB elimination. Stakeholders have called for the inclusion of pediatric-friendly sample types, such as stool, and the prioritization of new drugs like pyrazinamide in diagnostic algorithms. Performance criteria for TB diagnostics, including sensitivity and specificity, have been aligned with existing gold-standard tests like Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra. In summary, the global effort to improve TB diagnostics focuses on developing rapid, accurate, and affordable tests that meet the needs of diverse populations, including children and individuals with drug-resistant TB. These advancements aim to reduce diagnostic delays, enhance treatment outcomes, and ultimately contribute to the elimination of TB as a public health threat.
